detail.longDescription:
just a reminder that the 1960s american "global war on hunger" (of which the "green revolution" was a part) saw "the food problem" as two sides of the same coin. one side had "population" and the other side had "food production." (there was no side for "actually there's enough food being produced, it's just that people don't have enough money to buy it." or "actually more people would love to grow food, but they are dispossessed of land and resources", etc.)

so a lot of the "green revolution" modernization programs included family planning stipulations (including voluntary sterilization suggestions in india).

at the national convocation on world hunger in 1967, NEVIN S. SCRIMSHAW, from the Department of Food, Nutrition, and Science at MIT said in his presentation:

“The present rate of application of technical knowledge to food production in the developing countries is obviously too slow and will remain so unless new elements enter the situation..."

“Among these new elements must be greater progress in introducing effective family planning programs; in applying scientific and technical knowledge to increase the production of conventional foods; in reducing the enormous waste of food due to insects, rodents, and spoilage; and in developing new, unconventional sources of protein.”

"He said two approaches merit the highest priority in the problem of providing more protein. “One is the increased production of conventional plant, animal, and fish sources of protein... The other is the development and application of effective means of population control."

from the 1967 Oct. 10 issue of "foreign agriculture": https://archive.org/details/sim_foreign-agriculture_1967-10-09_5_41/page/6/mode/2up

they were full-on malthusians who saw the "war on hunger" as a literal balancing act between population and food. (and of course, they were worried that if there were too many hungry poor people in developing countries, that those people would go communist. of course.)

addendum: western environmentalism was the third leg of the stool in this project. groups like the club of rome were very into population control. to learn more, check out the chapter "Green Revolutions" by Björn-Ola Linnér in the book "The Return of Malthus".
